utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kryeziu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Questions by Mr. Lukic will now continue. Please remember that the solemn declaration to tell the truth, which you gave at the beginning of your evidence, will continue to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the court transcriber tells me she's not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nor am I at the moment, Mr. Hannis. Can we try the question again, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No interpretation again, as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the explanation appears to be the absence of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kryeziu. Maybe we can proceed this way. Have you ever heard of a name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you can, because there's no translation of the answer into English, which is fundamental, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the Albanian interpreters, who are doing Albanian to English, are here. We can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, I think the problem is now resolved, Mr. Lukic, so please start again with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try again. The name is Xhimshit Krasniqi. Are you aware of that name and are you aware of the fact that he had the war name "White Bear"?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him, and I never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you haven't heard that he was the leader of the KLA in your region. Have you heard of Rifat Sulejmani, former officer in the Army of Yugoslavia? And he was also the OVK leader in your region.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of him, even through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Have you heard that the father of Snjezana Djordjevic, a local teacher in your village, was tied to a tractor and then dragged from Dusanovo to the nearby vineyard until he was killed? Have you heard of this incident?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that Nikola was dead. He was a teacher, but I never knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that on the 24th of March, 1999, there were Serbs in your village? Or had they all left the village by that date?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, at 2000 hours p.m., NATO air-strikes started and it struck the Serbian barracks. And the Serbs of Dushanove were mobilised in the Yugoslav army, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: Were there any villagers in your village --

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but because of the Serbian forces, we didn't dare come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's something not right with that answer, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can assume that women and children who were underage were not mobilised. What about your village? Were there any Serb women and Serb children on the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go out to see because we were afraid to leave our houses because of our fear of Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you know that there weren't any Serbs in your village on that date; is that right? There weren't any there because members of the KLA were attacking, and that is the reason why all the inhabitants of your village left your village.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, sir, there was no KLA in former Dushanove Arban neighbourhood and no attacks were undertaken against Serbian forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of your statement, you say: "At that time, nearby, there weren't any members of the KLA who would have protected us in a way." When you say "at that time ... there weren't any," tell us, up until when were the members of the KLA in your village?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were never KLA in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 6D104 displayed on e-court, page 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 you say that from a woman, whose name you do not know, you heard that Serb policemen executed Nebi Bucaj and his two sons and his son-in-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was changed yesterday to an unknown visitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, but I'm more interested in Nebi Bucaj and his sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of his sons was called Enver; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document that we're going to see on our screens now, on page 41 of this book "Fenikset e Lirise," in position number 2 we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's obviously not that page. It's page 39, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 39 in the e-court, and that's exactly the page I need, Your Honour. Only we have to make one correction into the transcript. After my question on page 4, line 13, I got the answer "Yes," and then the next line marked as an answer is actually a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kryeziu, we have agreed that the name of one of the sons of Nebi Bucaj is Enver.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to a page of this book, 39 in the e-court, and it has number 41 on top of the -- page 41 of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's two pages earlier than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have it now. Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Page 5, line 1, I believe the witness said "Yes," but there's no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He did say yes, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we enlarge to see the second name from the top better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I think it's clear enough, Mr. Lukic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kryeziu, this is a book that has been used before in this trial. The publishers are ethnic Albanians from Kosovo. The names of fallen members of the KLA are listed. Concerning Enver Nebi Bucaj, we read that he was born and died in Dusanovo. Do you know that Enver Bucaj, father's name Nebi, got killed in combat in Dusanovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enver Bucaj and his father, Nebi Bucaj, and Ymer Bucaj and a friend Ferit from Randobrava, they were killed as civilians. I didn't see them, but half an hour ago I saw these civilians because my land borders his land. But whether he was a soldier or not, this I cannot say. I can only say that I never saw him dressed in military uniform. At that moment, they were all civilians. And I saw it with my eyes when they took the father, because the house is close to my house, and the police and the army killed him. We saw the tanks, the APCs of the army and the police shooting at the houses, at the doors. And when they took away my car, I heard from a woman that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've seen it in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could both of you just hold on. What do you mean, Mr. Kryeziu, when you say "I saw it with my eyes when they took the father ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, who took him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nebi Bucaj, the father, was taken by Serbian police and soldiers. I was about 50 metres away from the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they made him go inside the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again there was a clear answer of yes. I can hear the witness saying "po" in answer to questions which are not being interpreted. Are you sitting close enough to the microphone? You, perhaps, are not. So could you come forward a little, please. The usher will also adjust the microphone, which I don't think has been done properly, so that the interpreters can hear this clearly. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kryeziu, in your statement, the paragraph subsequently marked as 12, you do not mention that you personally saw it; instead, you say: "As we were travelling, from a woman, whose name I ignore, I heard that Serb policemen had executed Nebi Bucaj and his two sons," and so on. You have reviewed this statement; you have made certain corrections -- excuse me. Can I just finish. You have made certain corrections to the part where you say that it was not Nebi's son-in-law but a visitor. You did not correct it to the effect that you had seen it personally. It remained standing that you had heard it from a woman whose name you don't know. Today you are telling us that you saw that with your own eyes. Both cannot be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the foundation for that question is not correct, Mr. Lukic. All he has said is that he saw the father being taken away. He hasn't claimed to have seen his fate, nor has he claimed to have seen anything happening to the two sons or to the visitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to Nebi Bucaj and how his sons died?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How can you then claim that one of his sons did not get killed as a member of the KLA when you don't know how he died?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because half an hour ago I saw him dressed in civilian clothes, and he was not dressed in military uniform at that time. But he was barbarously killed at home, and, as His Honour said, I saw only the father being taken, Nebi Bucaj, from the stairs and asked to go inside. And I know no further. But from that woman, as I said yesterday and today, I heard that Nebi Bucaj and his two sons and the visitor were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that you do not know whether the son of Nebi Bucaj, Enver, got killed in fighting? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not killed in fighting, but he was killed at home. He was massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you heard that from a woman whose name you don't know.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you something, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The heading "Vendrenia" in the book is the place, is it, of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that one is place of death and the other one is place of birth, and here we can see both places are Dusanovo. So maybe the witness can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, Mr. Kryeziu -- in fact, if you look at the screen, you'll see that there are headings on this page, and the one on the right-hand side, the heading on the right-hand column, could you read that, please. Just the single word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Vendrenia" means the place he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, if you've got a version of events explaining that this happened in combat, then perhaps that should emerge at this stage to give proper notice; but if all you're going on is the fact of "death in Dusanovo" and general information about conflict in the area, then are you really putting to the witness anything inconsistent with his evidence? I mean, he may have jumped to conclusions; we can all see that. But are you really putting in anything inconsistent with what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this book is about the killed KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but is it those killed in combat or is it those killed as the result of events over a certain period of time, identifying those killed as having some connection with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we haven't translated this book yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and probably it will be clearer when we have the translation how come all these names ended up in this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it just sounds to me as though, perhaps, you're putting a question too far in the propositions you're putting to the witness, and what will help us best is if we can get factual information -- as much factual information as possible to see the limitations of the knowledge of individual witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished with this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, Mr. Kryeziu, paragraph 6, you say that you had heard that Serbs broke into houses and burned them down from the 28th of March, 1998, in Lez, Vrinje, Leskovec, Hoca.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, because on the 28th of March, from our houses, because that part is situated across the place where my house is, we saw flames and smoke coming out of that place. But that day, when we went to -- on the way to Albania, when the Serbs drove us out, we saw flames and smoke because we passed nearby. Those houses were shelled between Landovice and Dushanove villages; the place is called vineyards. And I worked there myself. We could see the military tanks attacking Suhareke, Rahovec, and Vrrin, but there were certainly police and military who set fire to these houses, at least this is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excellent. You have just told us that those places actually face the place where you lived. So you were able to see them before, to observe them before, so you must know that Lez, Leskovec, and Hoca, were major strongholds of the KLA; correct? And these fires were, in fact, a result of fierce combat between Serb forces and the KLA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was fighting, but the Serbian army had to fight against the KLA soldiers and not against civilian population - men, women, elderly people or children - and to commit massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kryeziu, shall we agree that if KLA members within villages -- are located within villages, then combat must occur within villages?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but an army should fight against an army, not against the civilian population. The Serbian army should find out where the KLA was positioned, and they should fight against each other and not against the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that on that day nothing happened to you or your family, but you describe that the village was surrounded; the salvoes were fired; fire targeted houses; shots were fired in the air; there was shooting all around. How many people were killed on that day in your village, if there was shooting all around?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only four people got killed at that moment; Nebi Bucaj, as I said, with his sons and his visitor. Then there were maltreatments, beatings, setting of houses on fire, destruction of property, and all such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those volleys of gun-fire, the shelling, was it all aimed at the village? How come nobody died if that really happened?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volleys of fire was addressed to the village. Houses were -- the doors of the houses were broken; shelling of houses took place, and you can see the traces even today. But fortunately, with the exception of these four people, no others were killed. But women, children, men were maltreated; that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the shelling and the mistreatment last all that time?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, because once the shelling started, I remember seeing a white coloured jeep. I don't know what make it was because I didn't see it carefully. I went into the house of my neighbour because we happened to be outside, without knowing what was going to happen. So the shelling started, volleys of fire, as I said, and we entered the houses. And I can say that there were over 2.000 police and army, but mostly they were army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something different now. You told us yesterday that you had seen that all the armed men had Chetnik caps and Chetnik emblems, cockades. You also said, however, that some of them wore stockings over their heads. How many men were there wearing stockings on their heads; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say men, I said soldiers. It's one thing to say men; another to say soldiers. I saw soldiers, not men. Of course they were men, but dressed in uniforms of the army -- of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you how many men did you see wearing those stockings on their heads?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't count them, but I know that when I -- that man with a long beard and long hair and a black stocking and the cap with a cockade, the Chetnik cockade, when I saw him I remembered that when Drazen Mihajlovic was captured, he thought that the Chetniks had come back to life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. We've heard that. So you can't remember how many wore those stockings.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, I'm just trying to jog your memory. All right. Fine. On the same day you say you saw Milos Scekic wearing the same stocking over his face; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but not a black one - I said it was a mistake in the statement - but it was light brown colour stocking, because I spoke with him myself and I asked the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We got that yesterday. But did you say that he had a stocking over his face?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he have a stocking covering his face?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you could still see his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You knew Milos Scekic from before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we lived together for 40 years. After I moved from Reti village to this village, we lived together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Milan Scekic a difficult, volatile man?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he prone to conflicts with other people? Was he inclined to pick fights?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, we lived in very good terms with all the Serbs in the village, but they joined the ranks when the war started. He had maltreated me and my son even earlier with other policemen, but as I said, before the war we used to live in very good terms together. Although that happened during the war, if I see him today, I would greet him and I would still be friends with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that before the war broke out an explosive device was thrown at his estate?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that Milos Scekic himself threw this explosive device through the wall of a neighbour. Together with Nikola, that I mentioned, I heard that they threw this bomb with a purpose of creating some unrest among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Milos Scekic threw an explosive device on his own property; is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know myself, but I heard that he threw this bomb. If that bomb was thrown by an Albanian, he would have probably got caught. As I said, there were over 1.200 houses in the village, and considering what happened, I think that the population quite lived with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you speak to Scekic?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 28th of March, I asked Milos Scekic to allow me to use one of the cars because my brother was an invalid; however, he did not allow me to use one of the cars. And, as I said, immediately after, some Chetniks surrounded me and threatened me with knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while you were talking to Scekic, he had his face covered by a stocking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, women's stockings, light brown. I could recognise his face because I knew him very well, and I addressed him with "Commander." And he said, "I'm not a commander. I'm a military person." And when I told him, "I know who you are. You are Milos Scekic," and as soon as I said that, these people with beards approached me and threatened me with knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And masked with that stocking, he was just talking to you and telling you that you can't use -- you can't use your car.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took my car, the car keys, the 3.800 Deutschemarks that we had, the gold from the women. Everything remained in the car. And as I said, my late wife tried to get something from the boot of the car, and someone then hit her with the automatic rifles. She lost consciousness. We had some water with us; we threw some water on her face until she regained consciousness. We waited and then we proceeded towards the border. And my brother, though handicapped, he walked on crutches up to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was anybody else present while you were talking to Scekic on that occasion? That's the only -- the last thing I want to know about this.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many, because it was a large convoy of people, and in addition there were soldiers and policemen. I said there were 2.000 of them, but maybe there were even more, because the village road is quite wide and there are other junctions nearby, three or four different junctions leading to different places, and all these roads were covered with soldiers, policemen, and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kryeziu. I have no other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to add one thing. They were asking for my eldest son, Bekim Kryeziu, and they would curse our Albanian mother. And that was something we couldn't bear. We could bear everything else, but not when they were cursing our Albanian mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kryeziu. My name is Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law. I would like to ask you a few questions. In paragraph 4 of your statement, you speak about the period up to August 1999, and this same Milos Scekic, commander of the police, comes to the village and inquires about the weapons. Do you know that in September 1998, more precisely on the 15th of September, several rifles, in fact 25 rifles, were surrendered in the village, one mortar, and a number of shells were hand-held rocket-launchers? Do you know that, Mr. Kryeziu?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Milos Scekic, together with another commander, Denic, whom I used to drive together with a Serb and Albanian policeman - we lived together very well - in the past, they came in civilian clothes. He even had one of his arms bandaged. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kryeziu, I'll try to phrase my questions concisely and clearly, and I would appreciate shorter answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kryeziu, the question was very specific, that it was said that weapons, and they were described, were surrendered in your village on the 15th of September, 1998, including 25 rifles, a mortar, a number of shells. Now, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that there were weapons at all or that someone surrendered weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kryeziu, do you know whether a considerable quantity of rifles, machine-guns, hand-held rocket-launchers, uniforms, and so on, were distributed in other villages nearby? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Apart from the village of Dusanovo, or rather, near the village of Dusanovo, the main Prizren-Djakovica road passes, as well as a railway line. Have you heard of incidents on that route when civilian vehicles were shot at?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Fire was never opened against the Serb forces in Dushanove.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about Serb forces; I asked you about civilians travelling next to Dusanovo on the Prizren-Djakovica road in their own cars. Do you know of individual incidents on that road when fire was opened on civilian vehicles? That was my question, Mr. Kryeziu.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no information about these incidents. I've never heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When you were leaving Dusanovo around that day, you heard bombing, and the barracks in Prizren was being targeted, as well as other locations near Prizren and not far from Dusanovo. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't know the barracks you're talking about. I don't remember what these barracks are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you hear a single explosion from the 24th of March onwards? Should I repeat my question, Mr. Kryeziu?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any other explosions but for those by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you can tell what caused an explosion by its sound; is that your testimony today, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this explosion occurred that you're putting to me. Which explosion are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you claimed that on the 24th of March, or rather, in today's transcript it says that you know that on the 24th of March, the barracks in Prizren was bombed. Now you're testifying that you don't know where the barracks is.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These barracks were bombed by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Apart from that explosion or explosions in the barracks compound, throughout your stay in Kosovo, you heard no other explosions?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could hear explosions every day and every night, explosions on behalf of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When you were going towards the Albanian border, you were stopped by a group of forces who were taking jewellery from women's necks. Those were the same White Eagles you had seen before, weren't they, Mr. Kryeziu?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mixed. I did not name them individually, but throughout the journey, they were taking all the jewelleries from the women. And I've seen this with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And, for the most part, they had rather long hair, some of them; right?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to count how many were there, but on one occasion I counted five or six with them. But we were going through a lot of trauma at that time. At that time I didn't know where my daughter was, where my son was. We didn't know where we were going. If I had a camera, I would have recorded that, but probably they wouldn't have allowed me anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you didn't see any insignia on them, did you, since you were traumatised, as you said?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't paying attention. As I said, we were trying to save our lives, because there were a lot of people in the column and a lot of young men were being separated from the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Dragulev.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kryeziu, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to come to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I hope I will not be misunderstood. I tried my best to explain everything. Maybe I did not explain everything in detail, but my great wish was to come here and testify to the events that I went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have a good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, tell us you're going to surprise us with a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no surprise. I understand that we will have General Loncar on this afternoon. I'm not sure what time now. I had heard 1345 and then most recently I've heard, perhaps, 1350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now been suggested 1.15. So when we rise just now, I'll make final arrangements with all the staff that need to be involved, in particular the interpretation staff, and let you know whether we might manage two sessions, albeit they are shorter than we've been used to, but perhaps overall a little more than an hour and a half. We'll see what can be achieved without going too far beyond 3.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I suppose I should alert you and the Defence at this time that I think I'm probably only going to be 10 or 15 minutes on direct, just to have him verify his statement and the supplemental information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the aim will be to ensure that his evidence does not extend beyond 1.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our overall feeling is that we should make use -- maximum use of the time available, albeit it's going to mean far more cross-examination than examination, and even allowing for the fact that much of it may well be in support of a positive Defence case rather than cross-examination of the statement, although that remains to be seen. But we do intend to set a deadline on the evidence that the witness will give at this stage, and if we run out of time, then the Defence will have to, in due course, make an application to bring the witness back for their own purposes and we would consider it at that time. But hopefully that will not be necessary. It may also be that part of tomorrow's time will have to be allocated to the positive Defence case. We will have to review that once we see the nature of the cross-examination; we can't determine that in advance. So informally, by e-mail, as soon as the position is clear, we'll confirm the sitting times for this afternoon. But what I can confirm at the moment is that we will resume at 1.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is General Dusan Loncar, by videolink, and we'll be presenting him as a 92 ter witness with some little live evidence to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to, first of all, express my gratitude to everyone who has assisted in making arrangements for this evidence to commence this afternoon, and to say to you, Mr. Loncar, that the Trial Chamber is particularly grateful that you have altered your own arrangements to enable you to come in today to start this evidence, because that will enable us to ensure that your own arrangements for treatment next week are not in any way disrupted. Now, the first thing I have to do is to invite you to make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your evidence will begin by examination, on behalf of the Prosecution, by Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Dusan Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I understand from your statement that you are a retired JNA general, you were a career soldier; that you are an Orthodox Serb; you're married, with two sons, and have four grandchildren. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you gave a statement to an investigator of the OTP named Annette Murtagh in March -- in February and March of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, this is Exhibit 2521.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, before coming to testify today, did you have a chance to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I received a copy in a timely fashion. It is in Serbian/Serbo-Croatian. I had sufficient time to study it, and the day before yesterday I was able to compare parts of my statement in the presence of a Tribunal representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I think on Tuesday, General, you had a chance to speak, via videolink, with investigator Jonathan Sutch and myself. At that time did you point out to us some changes or corrections that you wanted to make to that original statement, Exhibit 2521?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, and I am grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before today, have you had a chance to see Exhibit 2530, that is, the supplemental information sheet dated the 28th of November, 2006?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. I received it, I studied it, and I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, with those changes you made in the supplemental information sheet, are you satisfied that when that is read together with your original statement, that that is a truthful and accurate statement of your evidence; and that if you were asked those same questions, you would give those same answers now, under oath?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, one of the reasons we arranged for a videolink was because there was some health issues. I want to let you know that if at any time you need to have a recess, let us know, and we'll be happy to do that for you. I just have a few questions for you before the Defence --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- will have an opportunity to cross-examine you. In paragraph 21 of your statement, you mention Colonel Kotur, who was part of the commission on cooperation that met in Pristina. Do you know what Colonel Kotur's assignment was with the Pristina Corps before he came to assist you in working with the OSCE mission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Colonel Milan Kotur was a member of my team and my assistant in military affairs. Apart from this additional task, he was a member of the operations office of the Pristina Corps, or to be more precise, he was assistant Chief of Staff for the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 28 of your statement, you mention that sometimes when you would phone Mr. Sainovic to inform him about what had happened on the night before, you would learn that he had already been informed by General Lukic. Do you recall, approximately, how many times during your work in Kosovo that that happened, when you made your daily phone call to Mr. Sainovic, he had -- you learned that he had already been informed by General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Sainovic always insisted on being informed in a timely fashion as regards the latest events, especially if what was involved were important incidents or incidents involving a number of victims. As part of our daily routine in our liaison with the mission, there was a regular exchange of reports; however, General Pavkovic and General Lukic were under an obligation, if an important incident occurred, to inform Mr. Sainovic in person. This was to keep him abreast as to the events in the field, because he was the chairman of the commission, of the Federal Commission. Sometimes there was a need to contact General Lukic and Sainovic twice or even three times a day, but for the most part - I'm trying to recollect the nature of the incidents - it would occur two, three, or four times a week, when Pavkovic and Lukic were supposed to inform Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me direct you to paragraph 38 of your statement. You mentioned that Mr. Sainovic often came to Kosovo. Can you tell us, approximately, how often he would come to Kosovo during the time that you were there.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I can only discuss the period when I was in Pristina, in Kosovo. Depending on the intensity of contact with Mr. Sainovic, who was the then-deputy prime minister of Yugoslavia and the president of the Federal Commission as well as a prominent official of the Socialist Party of Serbia, which was at the time the strongest political party in Serbia, apart from other tasks concerning his duty as the president of the commission for relations with the OSCE, what I could say as regards all that was that he would come down once or twice a week. But, for example, in the case of Racak, he would spend two or three days in a row in Kosovo on incidents of that magnitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so we're clear, on the time that you were in Kosovo, I understand from your statement that you first arrived on the 12th of November, 1998, and then you left on, approximately, the 21st of March, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that time, General, how often were you in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Undertaking the obligation to participate in the work of the Federal Commission, which was a political body, I was in Kosovo for the first time in mid-November. Since the scope of activities of the commission included cooperation with the OSCE, the OSCE mission began functioning in mid-December, because it was at that time that they had a sufficient number of observers. Therefore, from mid-November until early December, I spent five or six days in Kosovo, or one week at the most. The rest of the time I was in Belgrade. There was no need for me to be in Pristina when my primary task was to liaise with Mr. Walker and other members of the mission. Therefore, as regards my work within the Federal Commission, I spent some 35 to 40 days in total in Kosovo. Since I am a family person with strong ties to my family, I tried to use any available opportunity to go to Belgrade during the weekend and then return at the earliest available opportunity, if there are no -- if there were no important incidents in Kosovo. Therefore, to sum up, a spent a total of 35 to 40 days in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during those days that you were in Kosovo doing the Federal Commission business in cooperating with the OSCE, how often would you meet? Would you meet every day that you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Meetings were of such a nature that we tried to deal with the current issues. At first, we worked on establishing channels and modes of communication with the OSCE; therefore, we met almost every day or every other day for a fortnight, because we had to discuss the issue of accommodation, movement, documentation, and the diplomatic status of the observers. Therefore, we first worked on the status issues. Later, apart from the basic tasks of the mission and its observers, we would have an average of three to four meetings a week, although there were days, on occasion, when we would meet once or even twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, generally speaking, who were the persons who attended these meetings, in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: As part of my team, its membership was constant; it didn't change. I always presided or chaired the meetings. With me were always Mr. Kotur, Milan, who was my military assistant, as well as Colonel Mijatovic, who assisted me in police matters; then a representative of the federal foreign ministry in Pristina, and that was Mr. Slana Velja; and an interpreter. That was the composition of the team. My secretary also took part, Mr. Rapajic, who kept minutes. As for the other party, in matters concerning Mr. Walker, he would attend and he would chair, or rather, lead their mission. And there was also Mr. Drewienkiewicz and some other -- and Ciaglinski, as well as some other people who were needed on a particular day. The most frequent people I met with were Mr. Drewienkiewicz, who was Mr. Walker's military assistant, and Colonel Ciaglinski would come with him, together with two or three other operations officers. This would account for the delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We understand from your statement and from Exhibit 2D8 and 2D9 in evidence that Mr. Andjelkovic, who was a member of the temporary Executive Council, was also a member of the Federal Commission. Did he take part in your meetings in Pristina in connection with the commission work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic did not participate in a single meeting, in any of the meetings of my team or the meetings that I chaired. He was the president of the temporary council for Kosovo and Metohija, and as far as I know, Mr. Sainovic introduced him to Mr. Walker. This was the first and the last meeting between a representative of the mission and Mr. Andjelkovic as regards the framework of my activities. However, I know that Mr. Andjelkovic saw some other OSCE mission people when it came to issues such as power-supply, water-supply, and so on and so forth. However, Mr. Andjelkovic never attended our meetings and never dealt with the issues that I was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Andjelkovic attend the weekly meetings in Belgrade concerning the commission's work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Sometimes he would attend; sometimes he wouldn't. At that time, the president of the temporary council, by his duty, had to be in both places at the same time, so to speak. Therefore, sometimes Mr. Andjelkovic would attend and on other occasions he wouldn't. However, I believe that he was there more often than not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with those Federal Commission meetings in Belgrade, you mentioned Obradovic would attend and report on VJ issues. Can you tell us Mr. Obradovic's rank and first name, if you recall it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I recall it well since I know Mr. Obradovic rather well. He was the representative and he was present more than other generals in meetings with Mr. Sainovic. At that time there was a change at the helm of the staff; however, he represented both people who rotated at that time. His duty was to monitor the situation in Kosovo. He was in the General Staff, in the operations administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: He was a lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the very last sentence of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, the interpreters here say they did not hear the very last sentence of your answer. Did you indicate General Obradovic's first name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. I ended by saying that his rank was that of lieutenant-general, and his name was Milorad Obradovic. He worked in the operations administration of the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Loncar. I don't have any questions for you right now. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General Loncar, the counsel representing the various accused here have a number of questions for you, and it's of great assistance, I think, to all concerned if we deal with these questions at this time while you're here with us. So I'll, first of all, ascertain the order in which these various counsel will address you. First of all, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The order will be: Mr. Sainovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the first counsel to ask questions of you, Mr. Loncar, will be Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, but first I'd like you to receive D08 -- 2D08. It is a decision on the establishment of the commission, and I will have a few questions about that. 2D08. The Prosecutor mentioned it a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it what's happened here is that you've provided detail, in hard copies, of the various documents to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we now have it, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, if you take a good look, you will see that it begins by stipulating that based on Article 42 of the rules of procedure of the federal government, the federal government is hereby establishing the commission. When the rules of procedure are used to base a decision, does it mean that this is supposed to be a working body of the SFRY government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was supposed to be a political working body of the SRY -- FRY government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that each of the members continue with their regular function, apart from being a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Their primary task is to continue with their regular duties and their additional task is to take part in the work of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have to wait for the interpretation, since we use the same language. If one takes a look at the composition of the commission, you see there Mr. Sainovic, who was deputy prime minister, and his deputy was Mr. Zika Jovanovic, who was the foreign minister of foreign affairs - first name Zivadin - and that there various federal ministers, such as the minister of defence, of internal affairs, of communications, of justice, as well as a lieutenant-general of the VJ and the Chief of Staff and the customs director, as well as the president of the temporary council for Kosovo. There is also the minister of the internal affairs of Serbia, the federal information secretary, and in addition, there was you there as well as the minister of justice of Serbia. If we have a look at those names, may we conclude that it comprised the top officials of the federal government as well as of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I agree fully, and it was structured in such a way so as to cover all areas pertaining to everyday life in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does this structure show the intent of the authorities in Belgrade to cooperate with the OSCE mission in Kosovo to the full extent?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Absolutely. In my contact I had with Mr. Sainovic when working with the Federal Commission, they always insisted on thoroughness and good conduct of the commission. I believe that was one of their priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since you were made member of the commission at a later stage, you were introduced into the commission because they sought to improve the cooperation since you had previously cooperated with Mr. Walker, who headed the OSCE mission in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, while I was employed with the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, and I was the corps commander there. Also, after the Erdut Agreement which was signed, which was annexed to the Dayton Agreement, I remained in the area so as to ensure that the greatest number of Serbs remain in the area of Eastern Slavonia and Western Serbia. The first administrator was Mr. Jacques Klein, followed by Mr. Walker. Therefore, I had a long and fruitful communication with Mr. Walker for over a year. That was the reason I was chosen to work on this issue with Mr. Walker as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this commission was a very high political body of the FRY government and the Government of Serbia rather than a command structure of the VJ, or of the MUP for that matter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Beginning with the fact that the agreement between the FRY government and the corresponding structures of the UN and Europe - and by this I mean the political agreement - anyone taking part in the process had his own political duties. I stated a minute ago that this commission was a political working body; otherwise, we couldn't have been engaged in implementing the political agreement. Therefore, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Sainovic, as the FRY deputy prime minister and the president of the commission, was a politician with the political responsibility for the cooperation with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I understood it that way. Having in mind his other positions outside the commission, which were of purely political nature, I believe this was also part of his political duties and activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, I conclude that Sainovic, personally or through you, conveyed the positions of the government and of the commission rather than his own position.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: On the 20th -- the 28th, this Tuesday, I was able to go through parts of my statement again, and I had previously described the relationship between Mr. Sainovic and the late Mr. Milosevic. When being proofed for this testimony, I was able to confirm that. Mr. Sainovic was a member of the federal government; he was its deputy prime minister. Therefore, anything he did within the commission was within the part of his duties as the deputy prime minister, based on the tasks and position he received from the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How are we then to understand what you stated in paragraphs 18 and 19 of your statement concerning the instructions you received from Mr. Sainovic after the mission was established? If you have the statement before you, you can review it again.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I do have the statement, and I'm looking at it right now, 18 and 19. In this statement - and I will not read paragraphs 18 and 19 - I spoke of Mr. Sainovic and his general attitude in his relationship with the OSCE, which was completely honourable, sincere, and professional. And he was trying to provide them with proper accommodation and all the other required conditions for a successful implementation of their mission. In every contact, in every suggestion that was tabled, in every assignment that was given, he insisted on a fair and honourable relationship; and I believe, therefore, that the commitment of all of us, and especially Mr. Sainovic, was to ensure that the success of the mission was complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Throughout your statement - and we can find it in paragraph 65 and in other places - you speak of the pattern of work, the procedures. Mr. Walker, for instance, would submit to you a major problem or an incident; you'd pass it on to Mr. Sainovic, and he doesn't give you his decision immediately. You say that instead a certain lapse of time passes. Is it the case that you were not able to give immediate answers because the questions had to be forwarded first?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just have a correction to the transcript. On page 34, line 12, it shouldn't be "decision" but "answer."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's been corrected, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So Sainovic was not able to give you his answer immediately because, first of all, he had to pass on the demands to the bodies that were in charge, that were competent, to resolve the problem. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing. The demands put forward by Mr. Walker on his own behalf or on behalf of the mission of the OSCE usually went beyond the specific points of the agreement. Mr. Sainovic, although he was not a formalist and he could sometimes react ad hoc, but he had to consult the federal government. Therefore, it took some time, and the answers concerning escort, helicopters, and everything else could not be given immediately, especially if it was not in the immediate jurisdiction of Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another problem. Page 35, the answer was not quite correctly recorded. Can we have the answer again. Maybe the interpreters can look at it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me the point you think that's not reflected, Mr. Fila, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, maybe -- on page 35, line 1: [In English] "... he could sometimes react ad hoc." [Interpretation] What I heard instead is that the witness said he was not an absolutist and he had to consult the federal government. Maybe we can ask the question again. This he wasn't a formalist, that simply wasn't said, and it wasn't said that he reacted sometimes ad hoc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Loncar, could you answer that question again so that we can clarify this difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was listening to your polemics, and I said, in fact, that since the demands of Mr. Walker most often went beyond the agreement, Mr. Sainovic could not behave as an absolute ruler, and he didn't dare and could not give answers ad hoc. He had to consult the federal government and on the basis of the responses of the federal government he could pass the answers back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could we say that Mr. Sainovic, in the government, was the first among equals, especially in view of the discussion of his role that we had before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: We had all the same duties and responsibilities and he was leading --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please, General. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object. I think that calls for speculation on the part of this witness to say whether Mr. Sainovic was the first among equals, without indicating who all the other supposed equals are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and it's asking a question about the government, which is not really a matter for this witness to answer at all. So let's concentrate on what the witness has knowledge of, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this witness was a member of the commission chaired by Mr. Sainovic, and when we ask him about his status on the commission chaired by Sainovic, it's not speculation and I'm not asking about the government. I'm asking him, as a member of the commission, how did a regular member of the commission defer from Sainovic, who was the chairman? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two things about that, Mr. Fila. First of all, the question you asked has been translated as: "Could we say that Mr. Sainovic, in the government, was the first among equals," so -- well, that's how it's been translated and how it came over to me and to Mr. -- please don't argue while I'm speaking. So you can clarify it by asking the question again, and if you're confining it to his role in the commission, then that question will be admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already apologised if I said that. I'm sorry. That's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the question is: Compared to other members of the commission - and you were one yourself - was Mr. Sainovic just the first among equals? Was he just the chairman or did he have greater powers than you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I don't know who could have powers over me, but it's a fact that he was chairman of the Federal Commission. And I hope nobody minds my saying so; in some missions and in some tasks, I held more responsibility than Mr. Sainovic. But generally I agree with your assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. If you were to describe --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think he's finished answering the question. Maybe it's because they're both speaking Serbian, but it sounded like he was still talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer looks complete to me, Mr. Hannis, and if you want to re-examine on it, you may. Please carry on, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have answered quite extensively my questions about the work of Mr. Sainovic. Maybe some questions will sound strange to you, but lots of people have been heard here and we have heard a lot of stories and we have to clarify some of them through you. If some things sound odd to you, you can believe me they sounded odd to me, too. But this is our job. In his work, was Mr. Sainovic conscientious?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Absolutely. Now, let me tell you - and I've said it before in my statement - Mr. Sainovic held great authority, both formally and substantially; formally in the sense that he had the official role of the deputy prime minister, chairman of the Federal Commission, and he also held the role in the party that he did. But in Kosovo, he tried to do much more than his various functions strictly compelled him to. He worked together with Mr. Andjelkovic in establishing the local authorities at that level, establishing the police force at the local level. And I would say, indeed, that he worked very conscientiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Fila. I'm only speaking about the time when I was engaged in that commission. I am not speaking at all about before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you, about that period from November to the 21st of March. Did you notice that he personally obstructed cooperation with the Kosovo Verification Mission, or did he give you instructions to obstruct it? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: That's a very strange question, indeed. If somebody insists in speaking to me many times that we should work conscientiously and seriously, that everything depends on it, that we should cooperate with the OSCE mission, that we have to honour all their demands, I don't see why I would act differently and especially obstruct the cooperation. It's not logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's not logical to me either.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: And, anyway, nobody can instruct me to do contrary to what my job is. I don't think he did it. He appreciated the efforts of all of us, and he invested a lot himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you concluded that Sainovic was committed to peace, not war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I think that was his mindset and his nature. He's a peace-loving man, not a warrior.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 76 you spoke of the fact that he was politically committed to establishing a multi-ethnic police force or army.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Police, all right. Was it his political position that it was necessary in order to appease the situation? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: You know, there was such high tensions. The situation was so fraught in Kosovo. It was very complex, and everything was possible. We needed to defuse [Realtime transcript read in error "diffuse"] that tension and defuse all situations. And the political atmosphere was such that Albanians accepted the decisions of Albanians more easily. They wanted their own police, their own authorities, and Mr. Sainovic understood that. And he achieved good results in the establishment of the multi-ethnic police, which was short-lived, unfortunately, in view of the events that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ordinarily, things like this would be caught in the review, but I'm not sure it will. Page 39, line 20, the word is "defuse," like take the fuse off the situation, not to "diffuse." And that may not be caught and that certainly changes the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note what you say, Mr. Ackerman. This particular English expression has always caused me difficulty, and there may not be any difference between the two. But I note the point you make and we shall take account of it. Carry on, please, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, in paragraph 30, I believe, you say that there was a meeting of the Federal Commission attended by Milomir Minic. If I understood well, Sainovic was absent then. It was at the time of the Rambouillet negotiations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it wasn't Rambouillet, it was Mr. Sainovic's visit either to Belgium or Sweden. Mr. Minic did attend then, and in view of the importance of the issues discussed at that meeting, although he was not strictly a member of the commission, he attended as a member of parliament, because after that meeting we had a consultation about how to organise a session of the Government of Serbia in Pristina. Mr. Minic came to the session for that reason, and it's probable that he, as the doyen, chaired as well. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In other words, the commission convened even when Mr. Sainovic wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: It was the only case. He was always there and he always chaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us now go through your statement. In paragraph 21 of your statement, you explain your first arrival there, your way of work. You mentioned the representative of the VJ, representatives of the MUP, and you mentioned Mr. Velja Slana from the foreign ministry. What I'm interested in is this: Did Mr. Velja Slana send his reports to the governments of the FRY, Serbia, and the provincial government, independently of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: You see, I had no influence on that at all. It was his responsibility, not mine. Velja Slana, and when he was absent, his deputy, attended all meetings between me, Walker, Drewienkiewicz, Keller, Ivanov, or whoever else, and they made their minutes and records independently of me. When they make minutes in five copies, we all read it and sign it. And it was their job to distribute the minutes. One went to the federal government, the republican government, to the provincial government, to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and one to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast. Both counsel and the witness are speaking to fast. We missed the last thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake in the transcript. Line 20 on the previous page, it was a session of the Assembly of Serbia in Pristina, not the Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was a session of the Assembly. I don't know if I made a slip of the tongue, but it was indeed a session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The point has been clarified. Please bear in mind, Mr. Fila, what the interpreters are saying about pausing to allow them to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The conclusion I wish to draw is that neither you nor anybody else had any influence on the contents of the minutes sent my Mr. Slana or the report sent by Mr. Slana, nor could anyone get access to these reports in order to modify or amend them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: We had a stamp. These were stamped and registered in the log-book, and nobody could alter them. They were kept in the archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs so that this possibility was absolutely non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, you say that you made some reports and sent them on to Mr. Walker, that you drew up such reports. Could anybody influence or change the reports you sent, or were they authored by you and do you abide by these?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, these were reports sent to Mr. Walker and the OSCE mission with respect to the territory. Every morning, the police and the army, through Kotur and Mijatovic, sent reports to my office as to what had happened over the past 24 hours, referring to any incidents that may have occurred. I simply compiled those reports, put them together without altering them. I stamped and sealed these and sent them on to Mr. Walker. These are reports coming from the military and police structures. Although the OSCE did not wait just for my reports. Colonel Mijatovic and Colonel Kotur sent their individual reports to the representatives of the OSCE mission by 700 hours. All I did was to put them together, give them the proper form, and then send them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The fact is that these reports were not changed in any way; they were just passed on.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, what would be the need? What need would there be to change them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Fila. In an earlier answer, when there was a problem with the speed of speech, you were telling us, Mr. Loncar, of the five copies of a minute that anyone at a meeting might compile, and you said that these went to the federal government, the republican government, the provincial government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and then the interpreter did not pick up the fifth one. What was the fifth one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The archives. The federal government, the republican government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Sainovic, and the archives, not the provincial council. Federal government, republican government, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Sainovic, and the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not Mr. Andjelkovic, not the provincial government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Loncar, this refers to Velja Slana's reports; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: It refers to the reports sent after the meetings between me and my team with members or representatives of the OSCE. The reports you mentioned a while ago, Mr. Fila, those were reports sent by the police and the army to the OSCE every morning concerning any incidents that had happened over the past 24 hours. So those were two different kinds of reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, it's not clear, Mr. Fila, what the answer to that question about Slana was, because it would appear that, while you were asking about Slana's reports, the answer you got was confined to where the minutes that were kept -- the minutes of the meeting were sent. Now, if you want to clarify that, you'll need to ask about it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At one point, Mr. Loncar, I asked you about the notes and reports drawn up by Mr. Velja Slana and whether these could be influenced by anyone. Your response was that he kept some records, that you later signed these, and that they were sent on to the five addresses you mentioned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that's one kind of report sent by you up the hierarchy towards the authorities of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last set of questions concerned the reports sent by the military and the police about the incidents occurring overnight, and you were to put these together and forward them to Mr. Walker. That would be a second kind of report.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, have I clarified that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With the exception of the last sentence in paragraph 26, at the end of the meeting I would make one report and we would all sign it. Is that the same one as Slana compiled? Perhaps it is; perhaps it isn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now clear, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I was in charge and I was the first to sign it, I spoke of it as my report. That's the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, you said that you were an intermediary between the commission and the OSCE, but in one sentence you say that you reported to the army. Mr. Loncar, does this imply that you passed on to the army information from the Kosovo Verification Mission and the other way around?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I have been a soldier since birth, so to speak, and of course my profession implies certain terminology. When I say "report," to me it's the same as "brief" or "inform," and that's how you should understand this word. It means to inform or to brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's how I understood you, but because various other interpretations are possible, I wanted to clarify this. In paragraph 25, you mention two occasions when Mr. Walker's requests were not met. This refers to personal weapons and the helicopter. With reference to the helicopter, you said that you informed Sainovic about this, and I quote, that after a while he informed you that this would not be accepted because it was not in compliance with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Walker's request and Mr. Sainovic's reply, would the cabinet have to make this decision for Mr. Sainovic to pass on? Because, as I understand it, it was not Sainovic's personal decision whether or not to provide the helicopter. Can you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
