utterances.text: With respect to the two questions you mentioned, the two issues you mentioned, in the dialogue between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Walker, there were specific proposals put forward by Mr. Sainovic. He suggested to Mr. Walker that he should consider our providing our helicopter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. Please stop. Please answer the question you've actually been asked, which is: Was this a cabinet decision or was it Mr. Sainovic's own decision? It's important you deal with the question, because we have your statement and we know what you've said so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Thank you. Thank you. I am convinced that Mr. Sainovic did not have the right to make this decision, that this was a decision of the federal cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to personal weapons, there were two agreements, as far as we can recall; Holbrooke and Milosevic, that's the first one, and the second one was Geremek and Milanovic. And the federal government was responsible for the protection and safety of the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Wouldn't it then have been more logical that if they wanted something changed, they should ask for the agreement to be changed, and then they could take care of their own security and own medical care rather than asking you for all this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: If I remember well, that's precisely the gist of what Mr. Sainovic responded. He said this is not provided for in the agreement. He said he would pass it on to the proper authorities and get a reply, and, as you know, the reply was negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As an experienced person and a general, the two pistols requested by Mr. Walker, to what extent would that have increased the security of the Kosovo Verification Mission, which numbered a few hundred people, asking for two pistols at this high-level commission meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I don't know what motivated Mr. Walker to request this. He probably felt personally safer if accompanied by two armed escorts. I would exclude the possibility of it increasing the safety of the other members of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All this talk of weapons, two pistols, was this actually evading the real topic, beating around the bush? Maybe that's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it is his personal opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop a moment again, Mr. Loncar. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. I'm having a hard time articulating what my objection is, but that calls for speculation and a conclusion. I don't know what "beating around the bush" means in this context. It may mean one thing to Mr. Fila and something different to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's right. The question is vague and it seems to invite speculation, Mr. Fila. I think we should concentrate on fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that case, would you agree with me that a helicopter owned by the army or the police of Yugoslavia, doesn't matter which, carrying a Red Cross symbol would have been sufficient to protect anyone possibly injured, who was possibly injured, and who was a member of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: At the time the helicopter was being discussed, there were no injuries, and more than half the members of the verification mission had not yet arrived. Our helicopter would have carried out the same tasks as the helicopter Mr. Walker was requesting from Switzerland, especially as it had the similar tactical performances.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If we take into account that no one had been injured, that the Kosovo Verification Mission was supposed to ensure peace and separation of the hostile parties, and ensure peace, how do you explain that Ambassador Walker was spending time on two pistols and a helicopter when all the helicopters owned by the Army of Yugoslavia, as far as I know, were of foreign make as well? So how would you explain this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, it's not an easy question to answer. I think that any deviation from the primary task for which they were there was a waste of time, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 30 you talk about the meetings of the commission. In the last line, there is mention of the VJ and the MUP. Would it be correct to conclude, from what you say, that the commission, in fact, dealt with incidents concerning the VJ and the MUP? And is that what you were referring to when you were referring to the engagement of the VJ and the MUP? Because you said that at the commission you discussed the incident.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: No. With reference to paragraph 30 and the sentence you quote, the question put to me by the investigator, if I remember correctly, was whether at the meetings of the commission chaired by Mr. Sainovic there was discussion of the work, tasks, and manner of execution of their tasks of the VJ and the MUP. So it was not that the VJ and the MUP were being discussed but their tasks that had to do with the commission. That's what is meant here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 33 you mention requests by the Kosovo Verification Mission to inspect facilities. I assume this refers to the VJ and the MUP facilities, so let us first clarify the negative reply passed on to you by Sainovic. Was that his personal standpoint or was this the standpoint of the Yugoslav cabinet? And did he tell you this as the president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I received the reply from Mr. Sainovic. I heard from other members of the Federal Commission that this had been a decision by the federal cabinet because no one, including Sainovic, had the right to go beyond the terms of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you aware that the negative reply given by the cabinet was motivated by the fact that before the arrival of the Kosovo Verification Mission there had been an organisation called KDOM on Kosovo? And are you aware that KDOM had carried out monitoring of the withdrawal of the army to the barracks and taken an inventory of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I heard this from Mr. Sainovic and I also saw it on the ground when I arrived. I saw KDOM there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know that the UN and NATO, with respect to withdrawal of the army to the barracks and the listing of the weapons, assessed this in positive terms, and then the cabinet concluded that it was not necessary to waste time doing something that had already been done and done well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I know that the KDOM report to the UN Security Council and the European bodies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the remainder of the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, you will need to give us your reply again; it was not caught completely by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure, Your Honour. I know that KDOM's report to the UN Security Council and the European bodies for security was the reason for the withdrawal of the decision on air-strikes in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So they, in their assessment, thought that our side had done this properly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, and that the agreement had been fully complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: NATO decision on air-strikes, line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 38, and in one of your previous responses to my questions, you mentioned an expression which occurs more than once in your supplemental information sheet. I believe it's found in paragraph 8 of the supplemental information sheet. So it's paragraph 8 in the supplemental information sheet. Can we clarify this a little bit? I will put questions and you will reply, and then I think it will be time for a break. You said, and I will quote you, "Sainovic had de facto authority. I'm not sure about de jure. I now believe that he got his authority as head of," that's what it says here, it's actually "president of the Federal Commission from the federal government and Prime Minister Bulatovic rather than directly from Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your question, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is the following: Were you here trying to say that his authority stemmed from the fact that he was one of the deputy prime ministers of the federal government and the president of the Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE and that was all, or did you mean to say something else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I have already said that Mr. Sainovic indubitably had authority among all the structures in Kosovo and Metohija, especially, I would say, he was the politician that was most accepted by non-Serbs in Kosovo, Albanians and other non-Serbs. His authority stemmed from what you say and from his personal activities in setting up the organs of authority and getting them to function. I've already said that. So he had de facto authority because that was his fear of competence, because he belonged to the federal cabinet, federal government. And this could not be, as I said in my first statement, that he got his authority from Milosevic. It was from the federal government, not from Milosevic, and we can all see and understand what the de facto situation is. As for de jure, it's very hard for me to speak about that. So what I'm talking about is the actual situation on the ground in Kosovo-Metohija and Mr. Sainovic's behaviour, which was at a very high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The last question before the break: The commission you worked with in Kosovo and Belgrade had no command authority. It wasn't the VJ's superior or the MUP's superior. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I did not command anyone. I had no escort. The only person I had was a secretary and a driver and my typist. These were the three people I could command, so to say. Other than that, there was no command, no subordination, no superiority in any sense, and that was the scope of my activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we should take a break since this is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it should now be possible for you to consider progress and formulate a clear estimate of how we're going to achieve the objective in this case in relation to this witness. And if you would communicate with the deputy in front of me during the break, that will enable us to judge how we should allocate the rest of the time available for cross-examination. Mr. Loncar, we need to have a break now for a number of reasons. We will be away for 20 minutes and we will resume again at 10 minutes to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, we are back in session now. Mr. Fila, can you give me some sort of projection? How does that compare with what you've done so far? Oh, well, we're doing well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Fila, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your testimony today and before, you stated that in the course of your duties you met Colonel Ciaglinski and General Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since one of them testified and the other one will, can you explain your cooperation with them? And as regards each one of them, do you believe they were objective and whether there was a good-will on their part, based on your conclusions and working with them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I know the two aforementioned gentlemen well. Speaking professionally, these were professional officers, true professionals, who were fair, and especially I mean Mr. Ciaglinski. As I said, on the 28th of this month, when I was being proofed for this testimony, I told -- I was under the impression that Mr. Drewienkiewicz was much more inclined towards the Albanians and biased against the Serbs. He tried not to give away that impression, but in some of the contacts we had, when he would get angry, it seemed that we were always the ones to blame. I was under the impression that he was more tolerant to the other party. As for any other aspects of his behaviour, both of them were men of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that while the KVM was in Kosovo, the KLA gained in strength and the number of their ambushes increased?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I can also corroborate it with the fact that it was Drewienkiewicz's assessment as well and Mr. Ciaglinski's assessment, and they expressed them during our meetings which we had during various incidents. From one day to the next, more and more territory was controlled by the Albanians. We were also informed that their units were growing, because by that time they had formed brigades and zone staffs. They intensified their attacks which grew in strength. They had better weaponry. They had the so-called Black Arrow snipering rifles coming from the west. Therefore, I agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did our side, so to say, have any suspicion as to the leaks from the mission towards the KLA? And that's how the KLA knew when convoys would pass through and when to attack. Was this a presumption on our part?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer such a question. It was their opinion, when I talked to Ivanov and Mr. Keller, as well as to Drewienkiewicz, that they had two types of verifiers: Those who were professional and those who did something else. I don't know what was degree of their insight, but it was obvious that the KLA knew in advance what we were doing and how we were doing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At a certain point in your statement, you say that you asked for the KLA to be called terrorists since they kidnapped, robbed, and killed from ambush, because these were undoubtedly terrorist acts. What was the reaction on the side of the mission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Even today, as a professional soldier, I tend to -- I tend not to express my views; however, I deemed all those to be terrorist acts whenever the opposing side acted. The verifiers, and especially the top officials of the mission, you always refer to them as the KLA or the OVK. Only on several occasions, such as when a hand-grenade was thrown into a bar in Pristina where 13 Serbian kids were killed, that was the only instance when they referred to it as a terrorist act. It happened on a few occasions, but I never heard Mr. Walker or anyone else say "terrorist acts" or "terrorist forces." On the contrary. I heard this on two or three occasions from Ciaglinski and once from Drewienkiewicz. They were only prone to use the KLA or the OVK term.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did our side believe, therefore, that the KVM was trying to minimise, to downplay, the importance of the KLA activities and at the same time displaying their bias? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I thought about it a lot. They never accepted my proposition, although at every meeting I always referred to them as terrorist forces, terrorist acts; however, they always used the other term. With hindsight, I could say that they were applying the criteria used these days. At that time, when you had terrorist acts against property and civilians, it was supposed to have been called terrorism; however, any action taken against the police or the army, they deemed not to be terrorist but, rather, actions undertaken by a liberation army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, from a personal point of view, I entirely understand what you're saying, but I wonder if I could ask you to consider this: That, rightly or wrongly, agreement had been reached between the federal authorities and the OSCE, which involved monitoring the conduct of two sides: The forces for which you were the liaison and the OSCE had, on the other side, contact with the forces ranged against you, which you call terrorists - they occasionally did - but they were more commonly known as the KLA. Perhaps they saw a difficulty in trying to restrain or have any influence upon the activities of the KLA if they branded them as terrorists. Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, absolutely. I agree it is a possibility; however, I think it would have been fair on their part to have addressed it differently. We asked them not to insist on it; however, it was never accepted. And, of course, there is always a possibility such as the one you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This was the last of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, my name is Djuro Cepic, one of the counsel for Mr. Vladimir Lazarevic, and I will have a few questions for you. You mentioned the work of the federal cabinet and the commission that you were a member of. Am I correct in saying that one of the basic tasks of the commission, pursuant to the intention of the federal government, was to distinguish between the members of the so-called KLA, who conducted terrorist acts, and the other citizens of Kosovo and Metohija, irrespective of their ethnic or religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It was also one of the basic reasons why you asked for the so-called UCK to be called by its proper name, to be termed properly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You also state that you had cooperation with the representative of the Pristina Corps, Colonel Kotur, and the representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Colonel Mijatovic; that you received daily reports on the situation in the units and about the events and cooperation with the OSCE mission. The reports you used to receive from the Pristina Corps or, to be more exact, from its representative, were they clear, precise, and true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I never had any objections or any reason to deny what was put forth, and the OSCE representatives never contradicted anything that was in the reports of the Pristina Corps. It was always done in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The topic I wanted to put some questions to you concerns the chain of command. We heard a witness here; it was Mr. Ciaglinski. And we have Mr. Drewienkiewicz's statement. In part of his statement, he says that Mr. Loncar did not issue any orders to the army but that he is convinced that you were consulted before any VJ actions or activities. Mr. Drewienkiewicz states that there are indications that in Rogovo you were part of the police command chain. He states: "Loncar was within the police chain of command." Mr. Loncar, were you part of any chain of command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: In full responsibility, I claim that I did not order anyone; I had no authority to. And this is a lie, a misinformation. As for Rogovo, I was there on the spot because I was summoned there by Mr. Sainovic. He told me, "Loncar, go there, so as not to have another Racak again." I went there urgently, escorted by my secretary and by my driver. I found OSCE personnel there as well as Mr. Drewienkiewicz. I toured the whole site, and in the presence of some TV journalists, I stated what my function was; that I came there as an arbiter to try and determine who was to blame and to try and investigate the indications and the leads there. At the conclusion of that, both Mr. Drewienkiewicz and I gave a statement to the BBC, I believe. Other than that, there's nothing further for me to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In one part of your statement, in paragraph 42, you state that all orders and commands came from the Pristina Corps towards the 3rd Army and then up to the General Staff. The army had its own chain of command and the MUP had its own. While I was there, the MUP never commanded the army -- the MUP did not command the army, nor did the army command the MUP. My question is this: This practice is part of the lot that was in place, that each of the structures had their own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Absolutely so. The principle of subordination was clear and agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It seems I will need to pause between question and answer so that everything you say and everything I ask can be entered in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was a part of an earlier question of Mr. Cepic, which I don't think was answered, which referred to an impression that Drewienkiewicz had that the army consulted with you before taking action. Can you think of any basis that DZ would have had for forming that impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was his opinion, and I refute it completely. I believe his reason to conclude that was the incident of our nine soldiers who had been captured. Everyone was concerned then, including General Pavkovic, who was the then-corps commander and his Chief of Staff, General Lazarevic, at the time. For justified reasons, both generals called me almost every half-hour, every full hour, asking me, "What is the mission about to do?" and whether these soldiers would be liberated or not. I had frequent contact with Pavkovic and Lazarevic. Therefore, Mr. Drewienkiewicz must have asked himself how come I have such contacts which were frequent, although I was not part of the chain of command. But I can reiterate that I never wanted to take part in that. I was a retired general. This concerns the Pristina Corps, and I had no authority of command. And I was never consulted on any such matters, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is it standard practice, is it a regular occurrence, and is it something inevitable in the situation of terrorism as it was in Kosovo, that there is an exchange of intelligence and other data between the Army of Yugoslavia, the Ministry of the Interior, and other structures, such as the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Not only is it needed but very necessary as well. If we use the illustration of the world today, just take a look at the level of integration of information pertaining to terrorism. And I can expand on it further. I believe it was very much necessary, and at that time we should have forwarded some information to the general public as well, and we may not have done it properly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In such conditions of daily terrorist attacks from Albania across the state border, as well as the bringing in of weapons and equipment and the incursions of new terrorist forces, according to the law, the MUP was supposed to be engaged in trying to defend and preserve the state border as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Absolutely so. To generalise or to speak in broader terms, the MUP would have been more inclined and better trained to try and control the border. As for combat activities, well, we can discuss that, but in any case, a full cooperation was needed between the two armed components of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, in the same paragraph that I quoted, 42, of your statement, in the last sentence you state that, in addition to the two operational chains, the MUP and the army ones, there had to be close coordination between VJ and the MUP in Kosovo. Since the highest state leadership and then, in keeping with their decision, the General Staff of the VJ, in a situation of increasing terrorism, accepted a plan that the army should support MUP forces in combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, was it necessary to coordinate the activities between MUP, on the one hand, and the Army of Yugoslavia, on the other hand, in order to accomplish certain missions successfully? Coordination, therefore.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: It was necessary and indispensable. And we have to proceed from the fact that the vehicle of combat against terrorism in Kosovo was the police force. I think it should have been otherwise; however, the army had its hands tied by the agreement and it had to secure facilities, and their larger components had to be stationary and only smaller units could move. The police force had to be the main vehicle of combat against terrorism. That's why it suffered great losses and that's why it was the victim of most terrorist attacks. If the army had a greater role, and if the coordination had been better, the combat against terrorism would have been more successful. However, in any case, the conduct of both the police and the army was in keeping with the agreement. The coordination existed, but whether it was sufficiently good and sufficiently mobile, that's another matter. It existed, in any case, but especially in a situation of combat against terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That raises a question for me. You're saying that the police had to take the leading role in combatting terrorism because the army's hands were tied by the agreement. Prior to the agreement, which I presume is the agreement in October 1998, prior to that, was it the army or the police that had principal responsibility for combatting terrorism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my statement and in all interviews, I restricted myself only to the time when I was part of the Federal Commission. As for all activities before that, I told you I was retired, and I also said, on the 28th, that before being engaged again on the -- when I was, the activities of the police and the army were only topics for me. As for what happened before, I was engaged. I hope you can find other sources of information than me, because I really don't know. In theory, I know what should have happened and how it should have happened, according to our rules and textbooks and our military literature in practice. But what actually happened, allow me not to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Loncar, I think you misunderstand your position as a witness in a court of this nature when you take that line. Your evidence is not confined to the witness statement you have given to the Prosecution; that must be obvious to you from the questions that the counsel for the accused have already been asking you. And it's open to the Tribunal to ask you any question that it considers you can answer. You were not engaged in Kosovo and may not have knowledge of the position, but if you do have knowledge of the position prior to 1998, then you're bound to answer the question which I asked you, which is: Which force, was it police or army, that led the fight against terrorism prior to October 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as to what seems logical to me, and from what I read in the media, it was the army and the police. But the army should have played the main role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Concerning this last answer of yours, of course you don't have direct knowledge; it is your assumption only, based on what you read in the press. Isn't that so, General?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: It is. I'm sorry, counsel. The first time in my military career of 40 years, on the 12th of November, I set foot on Kosovo. I had not been in Kosovo ever before that. So I wanted to say that to clarify. All the knowledge I had before that was based on media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in that entire time in Kosovo-Metohija, whenever MUP and army activities had to be coordinated, it was done at the level of cooperation, without disrupting the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Allow me to say this: Cooperation is also a component of control and command, so of course you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'll try to make my questions clear and specific, and I would appreciate shorter answers.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the rules of engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia, it is clearly defined that coordination within units or between different units is implemented on various specific levels and that's why it is not necessary to have a third institution doing it, or a special command, and it's not necessary for a special entity to assume centralised command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is a responsibility of the commanders at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You mentioned during cross-examination of my colleague Toma Fila that the so-called KLA built up considerably during the tenure of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Would I be right if I said that the territory controlled by the KLA also increased considerably, that the KLA took control of areas from which the police and the army had previously withdrawn, and that at one point it controlled almost more of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija than the MUP or the army. Is that true, General?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, and I said that during proofing on the 28th, in precisely those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this build-up of the KLA and the take-over of territories that had been previously held by the MUP and the army, was this ever presented by you as a problem to the KVM?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: We tried to put such problems forward, but I would even get information supporting that from Drewienkiewicz himself. He would say, "I see that they are holding lines far in advance of what they held yesterday."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So the general conclusion is that they built up their forces, their weaponry, equipment, everything.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Before this honourable Trial Chamber, the Chief of the General Staff for that period also testified, the Chief of the General Staff of the so-called KLA. In his testimony, he said that the number of fighting men just before the NATO air campaign was between 17 and 18.000 KLA soldiers. Do you have any numbers of the KLA's strength?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: I have no specific figures. I know on the basis of our rough assessments that the numbers escalated, that we had figures about 50, 60.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that the KLA took advantage of the presence of the Kosovo Verification Mission in order to reorganise, consolidate, re-arm, and re-equip and prepare for war against Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Those are facts, that during their presence in Kosovo it happened. Whether it was done with the help or without the help of the Kosovo Verification Mission, I don't know. But the fact remains that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one part of General Drewienkiewicz's report, it is said that in end March and early -- end of February and early March 1999, in the area of Nerodimlje, Kacanik municipality, the KLA mounted attacks simulating a refugee crisis and using civilians as human shields. Do you know whether the KLA often used civilians as human shields in their actions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: The situation was very difficult around Podujevo, and it confirms what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can I repeat this question in a different way. Such situations where the KLA used civilians as human shields were frequent.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Primarily women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the course of December 1998, you warned the Kosovo Verification Mission against terrorist strongholds in Decani, Malisevo, and Podujevo areas, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, in his statement, paragraph 114, stated that the KLA had proclaimed the year 1999 as the year of independence. At the meetings with the KVM, was there any discussion about the preparations conducted by the KLA ahead of the spring offensive that seemed to be heralded by KLA moves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: The press of the Albanian side also reported such things, and there was frequent mention of the spring offensive by the Kosovo Verification Mission, including General Drewienkiewicz specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You just mentioned Podujevo, and there was one incident that captured our attention in the statements of Mr. Drewienkiewicz and Mr. Ciaglinski and in your statement. At the end of December, more precisely on the 28th of December, 1998, a Serb, Milan Radojevic, was killed from Obranje village near Podujevo. In order to evacuate his body, the police was tasked and several policemen were wounded trying to transport his body.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, he was the last Serb in his village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, was it the last Serb that had remained in that village?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed in a barbarous way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the KLA in that area had expelled over 180 non-Albanian families?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski stated that in that area --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you find a suitable point, Mr. Cepic. Complete the point that you're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to say, I can stop right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. I think you, perhaps overnight, can consider the extent to which it's necessary to ask the witness to confirm things that are in other states anyway that are going to be tendered by the Prosecution and about which there doesn't appear to be any controversy. Now, we have to assess the situation and plan tomorrow properly. Can you tell me roughly how long now you expect to be, since you started a bit earlier than you expected?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Roughly half an hour, probably up to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Approximately one hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what do you reckon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's hard to say, not knowing what the other questions are going to be, but so far I would say half an hour, 45 minutes, just on Mr. Fila and Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I've got figures --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Plus Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know how long Mr. Ackerman is going to be. He was good enough to let the deputy know the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, some of my questions have been asked by others. I'm probably down to 15, 20 minutes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Loncar, we have to stop now because there is an Appeals Chamber hearing in this courtroom and we cannot continue any further this afternoon. So we have to continue tomorrow to enable us to finish so that your week next week is not disrupted. Now, I hope that you will be able to accommodate us. We understand the difficulty that that creates, but we're doing our best to ensure, if we can, that this is the end of your involvement with the trial. To make the position entirely clear, we would have to start at 8.00 tomorrow morning. Now, do you have to travel to Belgrade tomorrow or are you staying in Belgrade overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as it is, I'm going to stay overnight. It's not worth while for me to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful it. So we would be grateful if you could be available for us at 8.00 tomorrow morning, and we will detain you no longer than 1.00. That will be the end of your involvement at this stage, certainly, and hopefully your complete involvement in the trial. Counsel are doing their best to ensure all questions are asked within that time. So we thank you again for your assistance so far. Overnight, it is important that you do not have any discussion of your evidence with anyone. You can plainly meet with and talk to whomsoever you like, but one subject you must not discuss with anyone at all is either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give, the subject matter of your evidence as a witness in this case. The Trial Chamber now adjourns until 8.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
